Armed Conflict & Security
• Colombian forces ended a 17-hour supermarket siege in Cartagena, rescuing around 20 hostages; one gunman was killed during the operation. 
• Ukraine said a strike on Russia’s Savasleyka airfield damaged five military jets as leaked Russian data suggested nearly 500,000 war-related deaths have shifted national mortality patterns. 
• The US Army detonated nearly 10,000 pounds of unstable lead azide at an Iowa ammunition plant after evacuations, as NASA monitored the plume; officials called it a “success” amid public health concerns. 
• A string of cyber and hybrid threats drew warnings: France blamed an Iranian-linked group for sabotaging supermarket freezers, Europe’s defense sector urged resilience against sabotage, and the US FinCEN probed a cybersecurity incident. 
• SpaceX launched classified spy satellites for the US Space Force, underscoring expanding space-based intelligence capabilities.
Why it matters: Intensifying military, cyber, and hybrid operations—from hostage crises to airfield strikes and critical-infrastructure sabotage—are widening the conflict landscape into cyberspace and orbit while testing civilian safety protocols.

Geopolitics & Diplomacy
• South Africa’s top court overturned findings that exposed President Cyril Ramaphosa to impeachment over the “farmgate” saga, handing him a political reprieve. 
• A US jury found Huawei guilty of stealing trade secrets (but acquitted on racketeering), a verdict likely to heighten tech and trade tensions. 
• US politics roiled around Nvidia’s Jensen Huang: Trump said a pardon is “always an option” as lawmakers sought answers from US agencies on national security concerns ahead of Huang’s testimony. 
• China launched a corruption probe into Politburo member and Shanghai party chief Chen Jining, signaling Beijing’s campaign continues at elite levels. 
• Germany’s Friedrich Merz warned Russia is escalating across Europe and space as Washington shelved business incentives for Moscow amid the war.
Why it matters: Courtrooms and capitals are shaping the rules of tech competition, anti-corruption, and wartime policy, with decisions rippling through global supply chains and alliances.

Society & Human Rights
• Kilmar Ábrego García, whose wrongful deportation became emblematic of US immigration policy, left the US and arrived in Spain, amid renewed scrutiny of enforcement practices. 
• A fresh Serbian school shooting revived fears over firearm access and missed warning signs in the Balkans. 
• Fifty-three incoming US House Democrats will boycott a Harvard orientation in solidarity with a graduate students’ strike. 
• AI-fueled public records requests are straining small US municipalities, testing transparency infrastructure. 
• The UK harassment watchdog saw a spike in whistleblowing reports after Russell Brand’s rape conviction.
Why it matters: Immigration, gun violence prevention, labor solidarity, and the transparency gap in the AI era are converging to reshape rights debates and civic trust.

Entertainment

• Blade Runner 2099’s team discussed translating the film universe to TV, with streaming guides and interviews fueling launch buzz. 
• The Hunger Games prequel “Sunrise on the Reaping” led the US box office with a record Tuesday haul for the franchise. 
• Variety reported Sundance shorts programmer Mike Plante died at 56.
Why it matters: The culture sector is balancing nostalgia and new franchises while confronting the disruptive and legal implications of generative AI on music and film.

Why it matters: Tragedies test emergency response systems as corporate governance debates intensify at one of the world’s most valuable tech firms.

Science & Technology
• ESA’s Hera mission unveiled first close-ups of asteroid Dimorphos after NASA’s DART impact, while capturing an eclipse on Didymos. 
• Microsoft declared a “Code Red” overhaul after a historic Outlook/Exchange Online outage exposed engineering and recovery gaps. 
• Half of NASA’s aging Mars fleet faces technical setbacks, including Perseverance communications and Odyssey fuel constraints. 
• The FAA is probing an Amazon drone crash after a delivery incident, spotlighting growing pains in autonomous logistics. 
• Mathematicians are assessing AI- and human-assisted “dual proofs” of the Riemann hypothesis as journals and experts urge careful checking.
Why it matters: Space missions and cloud reliability are reshaping scientific frontiers and digital resilience, while AI’s entry into fundamental math could mark a paradigm shift.

Why it matters: High-stakes rulings and officiating controversies shape competitive integrity as national sides recalibrate for marquee rugby clashes.

Health & Pandemic
• The US Army’s Iowa lead azide detonation drew CDC support for risk communication amid fears of toxic fallout and environmental impacts. 
• US measles deaths rose to 14 as cases near 6,000, underscoring vaccination gaps. 
• Tuberculosis research identified a shared membrane defense that blunts antibiotic effectiveness, while the FDA is poised to approve the first in vivo CRISPR therapy.
Why it matters: Environmental health events and resurgent infectious diseases highlight persistent vulnerabilities even as gene-editing breakthroughs edge closer to clinical reality.

Economy & Markets
• Poundland entered administration, putting roughly 12,000 jobs at risk weeks before Christmas as its owner rejected rescue bids. 
• US inflation accelerated to 3.8% annually, fueling a tech-led sell-off; GDP was revised up to 4.3% annualized in Q3, keeping a December Fed hike in play. 
• AI market stress deepened: Nvidia and CoreWeave credit risk hit highs, and Anthropic’s shares fell below IPO price; investors fear Big Tech’s AI debt binge. 
• A US jury convicted Huawei of fraud and trade secret theft, while Dubai Islamic Bank agreed to merge with Emirates Islamic to form a $159bn Sharia-compliant lender.
Why it matters: Consumers and markets face mixed signals—firm growth but rising inflation and AI financing strains—amid legal outcomes that may reshape global tech and banking landscapes.

Artificial Intelligence
• Amazon and Meta are in talks to lift Amazon’s block on Muse, Meta’s AI shopping agent, after Walmart partnered with Muse to surface Black Friday deals. 
• AI data center construction is slowing under tighter financing and longer build times as Nvidia withholds support until facilities are nearly ready. 
• OpenAI research pegged a theoretical efficiency limit for large-scale matrix multiplication, while AI advances are reshaping theoretical physics workflows. 
• Nothing unveiled “Ear Note” AI earbuds with a case that records, transcribes, and summarizes calls, highlighting privacy and utility trade-offs. 
• Nvidia’s leadership saga continues: Huang faces questions from Congress and investors on Megaspeed while downplaying succession planning.
Why it matters: AI’s reach—from commerce and chips to math and everyday devices—is accelerating, but infrastructure, governance, and safety questions loom larger.

Climate & Environment
• COP31 post-mortems blamed fractures over finance and ambition as journalists parsed outcomes and small islands rejected the Antalya pact. 
• The world logged six consecutive days above 2°C over preindustrial levels for the first time, a warning sign rather than a treaty breach. 
• California braced for record king tides and flooding; Oregon footage showed dangerous surf sweeping beachgoers. 
• The Iowa lead azide blast drew environmental scrutiny over potential toxic plumes, while England pledged £11m to help coastal communities adapt to erosion. 
• A Guardian column argued no fishing method is truly sustainable at scale, challenging consumer “green lists.”
Why it matters: Climate policy gaps are colliding with real-time warming records and coastal risks, sharpening debates on adaptation, public safety, and sustainable consumption.

Longevity & Anti-Aging
• Socially active dolphins in Western Australia lived longer, suggesting group size stability correlates with lifespan. 
• Elevated bile salt hydrolase activity in the gut microbiome and klotho-targeted approaches emerged as promising aging modifiers. 
• A Nature Aging study found bone force loading extended mouse lifespan, while observational data linked antiprotozoal drug use to lower age-related mortality risks.
Why it matters: Insights from animal behavior, microbiome chemistry, and mechanical loading are informing new strategies to slow aging and improve healthspan.

Entertainment.title: Infinix Packs Its ZClip 2 Pro Earbuds Into a Snack Bag
Entertainment.text: The Infinix ZClip 2 Pro comes in a foil snack pouch, a form familiar to all. Tear the notched edge, hear the crinkle, and instead of chips you get a pair of metallic open-ear earbuds.The ZClip 2 Pro ships in air-filled foil pouches modeled on real snack packaging. The thinking is simple. Snacks and earbuds are two of the easiest everyday escapes, so Infinix put one inside the other and turned unboxing into a small reward ritual. Infinix calls it "Snack Aesthetics," and for a social-first generation that shares everything it opens. Where the industry keeps packaging quiet and serious, Infinix makes it loud and playful. The brand brings a sense of delight to everyday tech products through fun packaging and unboxing experiences.Each foil pouch is fronted by one of three art-toy characters, blending distinct style personas with playful snack pairings. The Streetwise Gorilla, wearing a street jersey and gold chains, channels the bold, loud crunch of spicy chips. The High-Fashion Black Rabbit wears a dark leather jacket, evoking the smooth bite of premium dark chocolate. Finally, the Laid-back Sheep pairs vintage leather with retro shades, matching the relaxed comfort of a classic sweet puff. Beyond driving the packaging's visual style, their distinct features: the gorilla's human-like ears, the rabbit's tall points, and the sheep's floppy drop, demonstrate what Infinix calls its universal "All-Ear Fit."The pouch is only the first step. The same idea carries through the whole campaign, built around "Clip on, drift away". Opening a snack and clipping on a pair of earbuds are both quick ways to step out of a busy day, and Infinix takes that idea out of the packaging and into the city. To launch the ZClip 2 Pro, Infinix turned ride-hailing cars into small mobile sanctuaries. Inside, passengers found plants, soft warm lighting, shelves of snacks and the new earbuds. They could snack, listen to music, call someone, watch something, or just sit quietly between the office and home. That ordinary stretch of road between work and home becomes a few minutes reserved just for yourself.The Airy U-Bridge sits on the ear rather than in it, using a nickel-titanium memory alloy wire that Infinix says has been tested to more than 5,000 flexes. Each earbud weighs about 5.5g, light enough to wear all day without pressure, and fits in perfectly next to your earrings. Every pack includes a signature detachable accessory that clips on and off the earbud. It's meant to be layered with whatever's already in your ear: minimal hoops for the office, heavier metal for the weekend, cuffs and studs in between. The shells get an NCVM metallic coating for a polished, jewelry-like finish, offered in three colorways.The hardware keeps pace. Dual 11mm PEN Dynamic Drivers handle sound, tuned according to the Harman Curve. A 4-mic AI ENC setup cuts wind noise on calls, and the earbuds recognize left and right on their own, so you can clip on without checking. Infinix lists up to 35 hours of battery life with fast charging, plus IP54 water and dust resistance. There's also real-time translation across more than 160 languages. The open-ear design keeps you aware of traffic on a walk, which makes it an easy pick for the commute, the gym or back-to-back calls from home.Tear open the pouch, clip them on, and treat your ears to the ultimate bite-sized escape. With the ZClip 2 Pro, Infinix proves that the most satisfying daily cravings are the ones you can listen to.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: Zamna Will Bring 10 Days of Global Dance Music to Tulum for Landmark 10th Anniversary
Entertainment.text: The Tulum jungle in Mexico has been integral to Zamna’s rise, hosting its first music festival back in 2017. Though the culture and hospitality group has taken the festival to over 20 countries since its inception, it returns to its roots for Zamna’s 10th anniversary with a special 10-day line-up in the ancient area. Teasing global festival-goers, Zamna launched a commemorative film last week, which captured celebrations from the last decade. From high-octane sets by renowned DJs Peggy Gou and David Guetta to theatrical productions that gave a stage to Tale Of Us, Rüfüs du Sol, and Gorillaz, the visuals traced iconic moments that fed off the “land, culture and history” to shape a festival that connects people and platforms dance music. For the upcoming 10th anniversary event, the group continues to cement itself as a global destination for dance culture. Turning the programming up a notch, the schedule kicks off on New Year’s Eve with a takeover from British electronic music platform RENAISSANCE. After welcoming Sasha, Maceo Plex, and Ida Engberg to the festival, Amnesia makes its Zamna debut, bringing a piece of Ibiza to Mexico for its own milestone anniversary. Other curated line-ups include ANYMA’s Berlin club night ÆDEN, Adriatique’s X, and Black Coffee, culminating with a special showcase from Adam Port of Keinemusik.  Alongside announcing the full line-up, Zamna has also revealed it will be partnering with UMusic Hotel and Beach Club in Tulum for the anniversary festival. Having built its local presence through collaborations with nearby institutions, Zamna’s latest partnership will elevate its efforts in hospitality by introducing a VIP experience at the property. Attendees will be able to flow from the festival space to the hotel with a new multipass, while also getting to visit special Zamna events there all year round. “For us, it has always been about the people. This 10th anniversary series honors a decade of shows, shared memories, and lessons learned, and we’re celebrating it back where it all began: Tulum,” shared Founder of Universal Xperience Fabricio Ledesma Heinrich on the anniversary.“Every detail is designed around the audience, and this time we want to raise the bar again, making every night immersive and unforgettable. This anniversary isn’t a finish line. It’s the foundation for what comes next, and there’s a lot more ahead.”For more information on Zamna’s 10th anniversary festival, head to its website now.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: LISA Gives The Nike Zoom Streak 3 "Black/Red" an Early Debut at the F1 Las Vegas Grand Prix
Entertainment.text: SummaryLISA wore an unreleased pair of Nike Zoom Streak 3 sneakers in Black/Red to the Formula 1 Las Vegas Grand Prix drivers paradeFirst introduced in 2009, the racing flat pairs a one-piece mesh upper with a Cushlon midsole and a Zoom Air heelThe sighting is one of the first public moments since Nike and Formula 1 announced their long-term global partnershipThe Nike Zoom Streak 3 got an early public outing in Las Vegas when global musician and Nike ambassador LISA wore an unreleased Black/Red pair to the Formula 1 Las Vegas Grand Prix drivers parade. Appearing alongside drivers Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc, she gave the public its first look at a colorway from the Zoom Streak 3 collection due in Spring 2027.The Zoom Streak 3 was built for racing, and its construction reflects that. A one-piece mesh upper keeps weight to a minimum and cuts down on overlays, while a Cushlon midsole provides responsive, low-profile cushioning. A Zoom Air unit in the heel adds impact protection without making the shoe heavier, a balance of lightness and performance that made the model a favorite among Nike athletes after its 2009 debut.The shoe's racing record backs up that reputation. Between 2009 and 2013, no earlier Nike racing shoe had been worn across more finish lines than the Zoom Streak 3, which made it one of the brand's most successful racing flats. Now Nike is pulling it from the archive and repositioning the low-slung silhouette as an everyday sneaker, and the Black/Red colorway gives it a sharp, high-contrast look.The setting for the reveal was deliberate. LISA's appearance follows the announcement of a long-term global partnership between Nike and Formula 1. Debuting a revived racing shoe at one of the sport's highest-profile weekends ties Nike's running heritage directly to its new motorsport partnership.The Nike Zoom Streak 3 "Black/Red" is set to release in Spring 2027, with release details still to be announced.Set your reminders and get ahead of what’s dropping next on Hypebeast Drops.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: Fred again.., Nike and Monkey Shoulder Lifestyle, Merch & Music Collective Stitch India's 2007 and 2011 Winning Kits Into One Cricket Shirt
Entertainment.text: SummaryFred again.. has teamed up with Monkey Shoulder Lifestyle, Merch & Music Collective and Nike on a limited-edition cricket shirt designed by Kunel GaurThe design merges the geometric graphics of India's 2011 kit with the blue of its 2007 kit, two winning shirts from Nike's archiveThe release comes just ahead of Fred's five sold-out India shows in DecemberFred again.. is suiting up for his India tour with a limited-edition cricket shirt made with Monkey Shoulder Lifestyle, Merch & Music Collective and Nike. Designed by Kunel Gaur, the jersey goes back into Nike's archive of India's championship-winning kits, combining two of the country's most recognizable cricket shirts into a single piece and adding the artist's own visual signatures.The base of the shirt comes straight from cricket history. Gaur takes the geometric graphics of India's 2011 kit and lays them over the bright blue of the 2007 kit, so two separate eras of the team's identity appear together on one jersey. Those years carry real weight for fans, as India won the ICC World Twenty20 in 2007 and the ICC Cricket World Cup on home soil in 2011, which makes the shirt a tribute to two trophy runs.The finishing details make it Fred's own. His distinct visual language is worked into the design alongside the Monkey Shoulder Lifestyle, Merch & Music Collective logo, and the partnership marks the first time the William Grant & Sons India lifestyle brand has named a Creative Partner. The result looks like matchday gear and works as tour merch at the same time.The rollout leaned into that crossover. Over the past week, the shirt has been spotted on some of India's best-known figures across sport, music, food and style, including Test and ODI captain Shubman Gill, rapper Hanumankind, executive chef Hussain Shahzad, dancer Ruhee Dosani, stylist Shaleena Nathani and longtime cricket commentator Harsha Bhogle.All of it leads up to Fred's December run in India. When tickets went on sale in June, the tour sold faster than any previous Indian tour by an international solo act, and all five dates are now sold out. He opens at Leisure Valley Ground in Gurugram on December 5, plays Mahalaxmi Race Course in Mumbai on December 8 and 9, and closes at NICE Grounds in Bengaluru on December 12 and 13.The Fred again.. x Monkey Shoulder Lifestyle, Merch & Music Collective x Nike cricket shirt drops November 26 at 1 p.m. IST exclusively on the Nike India App, followed by select Nike stores in Delhi, Mumbai and Bengaluru. Entertainment.text: SummaryDeborah Ann Woll will reprise her video game role as Faye in Prime Video's live-action God of War adaptationProduction is undergoing massive reshoots after Dave Bautista replaced Ryan Hurst as Kratos due to an on-set injuryThe casting points toward a potential third season aligning with the upcoming 2027 game God of War LaufeyPrime Video officially brought a familiar face to its highly anticipated God of War TV series. Deborah Ann Woll joined the live-action adaptation of the blockbuster Santa Monica Studio video game franchise as Faye. Woll steps into a role she knows intimately, having previously provided the voice and motion capture for the character in the 2022 video game God of War Ragnarök. Science & Technology.title: Mitsubishi Electric Research Lab CEO on How He Reached the C-Suite
Science & Technology.text:
The trajectory from researcher to top executive at a leading R&D organization doesn’t happen overnight. It took Anthony Vetro nearly 30 years to climb the corporate ladder at Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories, in Cambridge, Mass. He joined MERL in 1996, right out of college, and he has worked there ever since.Vetro probably is best known for his research in multimedia signal processing, focusing on video compression.Anthony VetroEmployer Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories, in Cambridge, Mass.
Title President and CEO 
Member grade Fellow
Alma mater Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn (now New York University’s Tandon engineering school) He became an IEEE Fellow in 2011 for his contributions to video coding, three-dimensional television, and multimedia adaptation.Mitsubishi Electric has moved away from making televisions. It now focuses on developing systems including ones used for defense, electronics, the energy industry, and space exploration.His ascension up the executive ranks began in 2018, when he was named a vice president and director of MERL. In 2023 he was appointed its president and CEO.He also works closely with the company’s new U.S.-based innovation facility in Cambridge. And he recently took on a dual role as deputy head of Mitsubishi Electric’s global R&D activities, including in Asia and Europe.Vetro credits IEEE with helping him develop his management skills after he served in several IEEE Signal Processing Society leadership positions. He also learned from his key roles in establishing international standards for digital image formats and video compression, he says.“Between my IEEE activities, standards work, and some of the business shifts in Mitsubishi Electric, I eventually graduated to more management leadership roles,” he says.A multimedia pioneerVetro is the son of immigrants. His father came to the United States from Italy and his mother from Sweden when they were both in their early 20s. They settled in New York City, on Staten Island.Although neither parent went to college, his father stressed the importance of education to his son at an early age.“My father started in the mailroom and worked his way up to eventually managing communication accounts and infrastructure for large financial companies,” he says. “My mother worked in banks, first as a teller and later doing bank reconciliation after pursuing some professional certifications.“Through their jobs, they saw people with college degrees getting better positions and promotions, so education was something really ingrained in me.”Vetro says he developed a passion for mathematics and engineering in middle school. He was accepted into the Staten Island Technical High School, a specialized pre-engineering institution. There he solidified his interest in pursuing a career in the field.“A lot of students didn’t know what they wanted to major in at college, but I knew fairly early,” he says.He was accepted into the accelerated bachelor’s and master’s engineering degree programs at the Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn (now New York University’s Tandon engineering school). He began his bachelor’s degree program in 1992 and the master’s program in 1994.“As part of the master’s degree program, I needed to do a thesis,” he says. “I wasn’t sure exactly what it would be on. Soon after taking my first course on image processing, I was certain that was an area I wanted to work in.”It was an interesting time, he says, because broadcast television was going through a major transformation, shifting from analog to digital during the early 1990s. It was long before streaming services, he notes.“I feel that industry-level engagement in IEEE is very vital to the organization in maintaining high relevance in the community and fulfilling its mission of fostering technological innovation and excellence for the benefit of humanity.”“The idea of being able to come up with compact ways to represent this very rich information was really appealing to me,” he says. “I’m also a visual learner. I liked seeing images, and there was some nice math behind them, too.”After he earned both degrees in 1996, Mitsubishi Electric hired him for its technical staff. He conducted research on multimedia signal processing, focusing on video compression.“The opportunity to work on projects around digital TV broadcasting and image processing attracted me,” he says.He conducted research in video conferencing, Internet and mobile streaming, and video coding technology, widely used for broadcasting, DVDs, and Blu-ray discs. He developed several technologies including digital TV receivers and displays, surveillance and camera-monitoring systems, automotive equipment, and satellite imaging systems.Another advantage of joining the company, he says, was that it allowed him to pursue a doctorate in electrical engineering, also from Polytechnic, while working.“That really sealed the deal,” he says. He received the degree in 2001.The road to managementAfter six years as a technical staff member, he was promoted in 2007 to manage the group working on digital video coding, processing, and streaming. Seven years later, Vetro became its deputy director, a top-level management position that he held until 2018.“After working for about 10 years exclusively on video compression processing technology, there were some shifts in our company’s business. Its overall strategy began to change,” he says, “so I became interested in broadening my experience beyond video.”He was asked to lead the lab’s speech and audio team. It was more development-oriented, he says, and focused on vehicle infotainment and speech interfaces before Alexa and Siri existed. He pivoted the team’s focus more toward research and established strategic paths tailored to emerging opportunities within the organization. Recognizing emerging trends in sensing and information security, he formed groups that worked on them.Mitsubishi Electric’s first U.S. innovation hubTo help spur innovation between Mitsubishi Electric and its U.S. customers, the company in June opened Serendie Street Boston, its first digital transformation hub in the United States. It’s colocated with MERL.The new office is modeled after the first Serendie Street collaboration space, which Mitsubishi Electric launched in 2024 in Yokohama, Japan.The word serendie is a combination of serendipity and digital engineering, according to the company’s website. Serendie is the digital platform designed to foster collaborations between data, people, and technology, it says. The space where people interact to extract ideas from the data is called “the street.”The platform brings together researchers, startups, customers, and partners to identify new products, test them, run pilot programs, and scale them up.Vetro says he’s excited about the endeavor.“Serendie Street [Boston] aims to strengthen the bridge between our global R&D efforts and real-world industry challenges. The hub is intended to bring our partners and customers together to engage in more cocreation activities, where we listen to their problems and work together to solve them,” he says. “I think the company has come to recognize that we can’t just do it all internally by ourselves.”The technologies being worked on include robotics, energy solutions such as integrating renewable energy into the grid, and more energy-efficient data center systems.The decision to colocate the hub with MERL offices was deliberate, Vetro says.“The area has a very rich ecosystem,” he says. “We have Harvard, MIT, and many other universities a stone’s throw away.”Strengthening IEEE’s involvement with industryVetro joined IEEE in 1992 as a student member during an event the Polytechnic’s student branch was holding. He enjoyed reading the IEEE Potentials student member publication and other periodicals, he says.“In the earliest stages of my career, IEEE was a place where I could attend conferences, read journals, and stay on top of the latest research and trends,” he says. “Over the years, I was able to build a professional network, which has been helpful. That facilitated a lot of research collaboration with university professors attending the conferences.“In more recent years, IEEE has provided a great platform for industry to exhibit thought leadership and discuss real-world problems we’re facing. I think these discussions may have even set some research directions among the academic community.”Vetro is an active volunteer for the IEEE Signal Processing Society. He has chaired several of its technical committees and conferences, and he served as an associate editor for some of its journals.He says he’s most proud of establishing the society’s industry board and serving as its inaugural chair. The board formed a corporate engagement program, launched the Industry Signals newsletter, developed short courses tailored to industry, and holds career fairs at the society’s flagship conferences.Vetro also had a hand in MERL sponsoring two IEEE technical field awards: the Flanagan Speech and Audio Processing Award and the Fourier Award for Signal Processing.“Industry-level engagement in IEEE is really very vital to the organization in maintaining its relevance to the community and fulfilling its mission of fostering technological innovation and excellence for the benefit of humanity,” he says.

Science & Technology.title: Blancpain Unveils New Watch Featuring the World's First 30-Degree Inclined One-Minute Flying Carrousel
Science & Technology.text: Blancpain, the world's oldest watch brand founded in Villeret, Switzerland in 1735, has announced a new watch, the Tourbillon Carrousel Inclined. Completed after four years of development, this model features what the brand claims to be the world's first one-minute flying carrousel inclined at 30 degrees.The carrousel is a mechanism designed to minimize the rate variations caused by the orientation of the watch. By housing the balance wheel and escapement—which regulate the timekeeping—in a rotating cage, it averages out the effects of gravity. In 2008, Blancpain introduced a wristwatch equipped with a flying carrousel whose cage makes one full rotation per minute. For this new release, tilting the rotation axis of that cage by 30 degrees ensures that the orientation of the balance wheel continues to change relative to gravity even when the watch is laid flat with the dial facing up.During development, multiple inclination angles from 0 to 35 degrees were tested, measuring amplitude and rate across six different positions. As a result, 30 degrees was adopted as the angle that best balances precision performance, movement thinness, and design. The newly developed manual-winding Calibre 222ISQ secures a 100-hour power reserve via two series-connected barrels. Furthermore, every piece comes with an individual chronometry certificate showing an average daily rate tolerance between 0 and +2 seconds.The exterior also boasts a major distinguishing feature. It adopts Blancpain's first-ever full sapphire case, with sapphire also used for the dial. The movement's action can be admired not just from the front, but from the back and sides as well. The entire movement has been thoroughly skeletonized so that normally hidden gears, barrels, and even the winding state of the mainspring are visible.The case is available in two versions: 5N red gold and rhodium-plated gold. The 30-degree inclined complication is housed within relatively compact dimensions of 40.30 mm in diameter and 11.30 mm in thickness. The two parts that make up the sapphire case reportedly take approximately 100 hours each to machine and polish.The movement finishing is not to be missed either. The Calibre 222ISQ receives a total of 210 hours of hand decoration at the in-house workshop in Le Brassus. This includes chamfering and polishing of 253 sharp internal angles, with finishes applied even to the undersides of normally invisible components. Moreover, the completed movement is assembled from start to finish by a single master watchmaker.The Tourbillon Carrousel Inclined will be offered as part of the regular collection, not as a limited edition. The release date and pricing for the Japanese market have not yet been announced.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast
